name: ooniprobe
why: Measures internet censorship and interference from your own connection, a real-world door into how blocking and DNS tampering actually work.

brief.what_it_is: OONI Probe is a free, open-source client that runs network measurement tests from your own internet connection. It tests whether websites and apps are blocked and measures the speed and performance of your network. Each run produces measurements that go to the Open Observatory of Network Interference, which publishes them as a public dataset covering more than 200 countries since 2012. The command-line client is `ooniprobe`, and the project also ships desktop, Android and iOS apps. The repository README says the CLI runs tests automatically every day once installed.
brief.why_it_exists: The Open Observatory of Network Interference describes itself as a non-profit free software project that aims to empower decentralized efforts in documenting Internet censorship around the world. The homepage frames it as a global community measuring Internet censorship since 2012.
brief.how_it_works: The README points to a measurement engine written in Go, a test helper server (oohelperd), and an experimental client (miniooni) alongside ooniprobe. The CLI also links a Rust static library (libuniffi_ooniprobe.a) from ooniprobe-rs, which the README says is used for user authentication. The install page says that once ooniprobe is installed it runs tests automatically every day. I did not find a detailed explanation of the individual test mechanisms in the pages I read; the docs site was rate-limited.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt binaries are available for Windows, macOS and Debian/Ubuntu, with instructions at ooni.org/install/cli. On Debian/Ubuntu you add the OONI GPG key and an apt source, using HTTP (recommended) or Tor as a fallback if the HTTP repository is unreachable; the Tor route requires running the tor daemon. On macOS, install Homebrew and then run brew install ooniprobe, followed by ooniprobe autorun start for daily runs. Building from source needs Go (the README pins a version in GOVERSION and recommends ./script/go.bash to fetch it), a C compiler such as GCC or Clang, and on Windows either WSL or the mingw-w64 cross-compiler. The first Homebrew step is installing Homebrew itself.
brief.standout: It is a real, long-running measurement network that lets an ordinary person see what is blocked on their own connection, and the results feed a public open dataset that anyone can explore. Its install page also sets up daily automatic runs, so it works as a background sensor rather than a one-off tool.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub repo (ooni/probe-cli) shows about 1,960 commits, 297 stars and 65 forks, with the license GPL-3.0-or-later. The homepage lists research posts dated as recently as 28 Jul 2026 and blog posts from 2026, including a launch of a new desktop app on 26 Jun 2026. I could not see a last-commit date or latest release tag from the pages fetched.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a marketing and research page, not documentation. The docs site (docs.ooni.org) returned HTTP 429 (rate limited), so I could not read the user guide. The Homebrew formula's caveats field is empty. Building from source is involved: it needs a pinned Go toolchain and a C compiler, a Rust static library that is glibc-based and cannot link into musl or cross-compiled builds without building from source, and mingw-w64 for Windows targets. The Tor apt route depends on running a tor daemon. Licence is GPL-3.0-or-later. I did not verify DNS-tampering tests specifically; the homepage describes testing blocking of websites and apps and network speed and performance.
